To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Tracy-Widom distribution is a universal extreme value distribution in random matrix theory, and that the Tracy Widom law is a non-universal law in disordered systems with heavy tailed disorder.

(i) the Tracy Widom law is not the only extreme value law that can be found in the context of random matrix theory; and (ii) the Gaussian disorder assumption in the context of mean field spin glasses is not always correct.

(i) the Tracy-Widom distribution is the correct one in many cases, (ii) in the presence of heavy tails the Tracy-Widon distribution is modified in a non-trivial way, (iii) the Tracy-Windom distribution is modified in the presence of correlations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of the extreme value distribution of the eigenvalues of random matrices and the statistics of the maximum of the log-correlated fields.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Gaussianity is a necessary but not a sufficient assumption.
Gaussian disorder is a good assumption in many instances but not in all of them.
the Gaussian assumption should not be taken as a dogma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the extreme values statistics of random matrix theory, and in particular the Tracy Widom distributions, are not always the right tool for describing disordered systems.
the extreme value problem is a key issue in the theory of random matrices.
the extreme value statistics is not a Gaussian one, but rather a non-Gaussian one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in many cases, the Gaussian disorder assumption is not justified and that the disorder should be considered as a generic heavy-tailed random field.
the disorder distribution has a crucial role in the description of the fluctuations of disordered systems.
, in order to make predictions, one should always be very careful in choosing the disorder distribution.
